results.result: The study analyzed longitudinal MRI data from 5718 participants (ages 4-82 years) across three cohorts (LCBC, ABCD, UKB), including 386 monozygotic twins, with up to 8.3 years of follow-up and 12,088 brain MRI scans. Sample characteristics varied by cohort, with LCBC spanning the lifespan (mean age 19.1 years), ABCD focusing on development (mean age 10.0 years), and UKB on aging (mean age 62.0 years).
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C5 and C82-C92 provide consistent and detailed sample characteristics across the abstract, results, and methods sections. The sample sizes, age ranges, follow-up durations, and demographic information are explicitly stated and internally consistent. Table 1 provides comprehensive descriptive statistics that support all demographic claims.

results.result: Birth weight shows remarkably stable and lifelong positive associations with cortical surface area and volume across all three cohorts. These associations were widespread, bilateral, highly consistent across lifespan, developmental, and aging samples, and appeared age and time-invariant.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C29-C30, C33, C63-C64 are strongly supported by the vertex-wise analyses presented in Figure 1 and described in the Results section. The spatial correlation analyses (C41-C45) demonstrate high replicability across cohorts (r=0.51-0.79 for area and volume), and the consistency is evident across all three independent datasets spanning different age ranges.

results.result: No consistent effect of birth weight on brain changes was observed across cohorts. While some significant birth weight × time interactions were detected in restricted and non-overlapping regions, these effects showed either unrelated or negative spatial correlations between cohorts, indicating that any effects on cortical change may be of temporary nature.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C38-C40, C46, and C68 are supported by the longitudinal interaction analyses presented in Figure 2 and the spatial correlation analyses. The lack of consistency is demonstrated by negative or near-zero spatial correlations (r=-0.35 to 0.04) for change effects, contrasting sharply with the high correlations for baseline effects. The visualization in Figure 2-supplements 2-4 shows largely parallel trajectories, supporting minimal interaction effects.

results.result: Birth weight had lesser effects on cortical thickness compared to cortical area, with no significant effects on thickness observed in the UKB cohort.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 are supported by the vertex-wise analyses in Figure 1 and the spatial correlation results (C45) showing moderate correlations for thickness (r=0.24-0.45) compared to higher correlations for area and volume. The absence of significant thickness effects in UKB is explicitly stated and visible in the figures.

results.result: Analysis of monozygotic twin birth weight discordance indicated partly environmental effects on brain characteristics. Heavier twins showed greater cortical area in frontal, temporal, and occipitotemporal regions (right hemisphere effects surviving correction), while lighter twins showed greater thickness in restricted right frontotemporal regions. No effects were observed on cortical volume or longitudinal changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C8 and C47-C52 are supported by the twin discordance analyses presented in Figures 4-5. The regional specificity and directionality of effects are clearly demonstrated. The finding that discordance effects overlap with regions showing birth weight effects in the larger sample (C47) supports an environmental interpretation. However, the meta-analysis comparison showed only suggestive (not statistically significant after correction) spatial correspondence between twin discordance and overall birth weight effects.

results.result: Sensitivity analyses demonstrated robustness of birth weight effects: controlling for education had little effect, controlling for gestational age in subsamples had relatively little effect, restricting to birth weights between 2.5-5.0 kg yielded similar results, and consistent positive effects on cortical area remained even when controlling for intracranial volume in lateral temporal and frontal areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 are supported by supplementary figures (Figure 1-supplements 2-5) and explicit statements in the Results section. These sensitivity analyses strengthen the main findings by demonstrating that effects are not driven by confounding factors or extreme values. The persistence of effects after ICV correction (C37) suggests some regional specificity beyond general brain size.

results.result: Spatial correlation analyses revealed that all comparisons of birth weight effects on cortical structure across datasets were statistically significant (p<0.05, FDR-corrected), with the topography of effects being comparable across datasets. Correlations were highest for volume (r=0.64-0.79), high for area (r=0.51-0.71), and moderate for thickness (r=0.24-0.45).
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 are directly supported by the spatial correlation analyses presented in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1. The statistical significance and specific correlation values are explicitly reported. The use of spin tests for permutation-based significance testing provides appropriate control for spatial autocorrelation in brain imaging data.

results.result: The effect of 1 SD difference in birth weight (approximately 600g) on cortical volume was 6708 mm³ in LCBC, 8466 mm³ in UKB, and 5980 mm³ in ABCD, corresponding to 1.2%, 1.6%, and 1.1% lesser cortex respectively. This effect is quantitatively comparable to 7.5 years of estimated age differences in LCBC and 6 years in UKB, based on estimated yearly cortical volume reductions of 895 mm³ (LCBC) and 1402 mm³ (UKB) from ages 50-60.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C62 present calculated effect sizes and comparisons that are explicitly stated in the Results section. The calculations appear mathematically consistent (e.g., 6708 mm³ / 895 mm³/year ≈ 7.5 years). However, the authors appropriately caution that this is an illustrative comparison and note that many factors influence cortical volume independent of age. The comparison is valid for contextualizing effect magnitude but should not be interpreted as causal equivalence.

results.result: The influence of prenatal growth on cortical topography is stable and reliable through the lifespan, appearing to affect the brain through association with brain reserve rather than brain maintenance. The 'offset effect' of birth weight on cortical area and volume appears persistent and consistent across the lifespan, with fetal influences appearing omnipresent in the spacetime of the human brain.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11 and C69 represent interpretive conclusions that are well-supported by the combined evidence from claims about baseline effects (C6, C29-C30, C33) and lack of consistent longitudinal effects (C7, C38-C40, C46). The brain reserve vs. maintenance distinction is appropriately drawn from the pattern of strong baseline associations without corresponding change associations. The language is somewhat grandiose ('omnipresent in spacetime') but reflects the breadth and consistency of findings.

results.result: Cortical surfaces were reconstructed using FreeSurfer v6.0 (LCBC and UKB) and v7.1 (ABCD), with vertex-wise analyses conducted using spatiotemporal linear mixed effects modeling. All analyses controlled for baseline age, sex, scanner site, and time, with ethnicity additionally included as a covariate for ABCD.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 accurately describe the image processing and statistical analysis methods. The use of different FreeSurfer versions across cohorts is a potential limitation but is transparently reported. The covariate selection is appropriate, and the additional ethnicity covariate for ABCD is justified given that sample's ethnic diversity. The methods are sufficiently detailed for replication.

results.result: Birth weight appears to have the most replicable and consistent relations to cortical morphology besides BMI, standing out as the single chronological earliest phenotype with such robust associations.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 is supported by the replicability analyses (Figure 2-supplement 5) and comparison to prior literature on brain-wide association studies. The comparison to BMI is supported by citations to prior work (Kharabian Masouleh et al., 2019). The claim about birth weight being the earliest phenotype is factually accurate. However, the comparative claim about replicability relative to all other phenotypes is somewhat strong given that systematic comparisons across all possible phenotypes are not presented.

results.result: Optimizing fetal growth may increase brain reserve for life, including in aging. Programs and policies to limit environmental factors reducing fetal growth may enhance brain reserve and prevent more people from falling below a functional threshold in advanced age.
results.evaluation: Claims C12 and C79 represent speculative policy implications that extend beyond the data presented. While the associations between birth weight and brain structure are well-established, the causal pathway from interventions to optimize fetal growth to improved brain outcomes is not demonstrated. The study does not include intervention data, functional outcomes, or threshold analyses. These are reasonable hypotheses for future research but are not directly supported by the current findings.

results.result: There was very high correlation between registry and self-reported birth weight in LCBC, and high reliability of self-reported birth weight over time has been found in broader Norwegian Twin Registry samples.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is supported by validation analyses in the LCBC sample (r=0.99 for 354 participants with both registry and self-report data). Claim C81 is supported by citation to Nilsen et al., 2017. These findings address an important limitation regarding the use of self-reported birth weight for most participants. However, the very high correlation in LCBC may not generalize to all samples, and recall bias could still affect absolute values even if relative rankings are preserved.

results.result: Prior research has established that a substantial portion of functional variation through the lifespan is of neurodevelopmental origin, that early-life factors are important for brain, mental health, and cognition across the lifespan and associated with psychiatric and neurodegenerative disease risk, and that birth weight reflects genetic and environmental factors affecting fetal and brain growth and relates positively to mental health, cognitive function, and brain characteristics.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C23 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for the current study. The citations appear appropriate and the characterizations of prior work are consistent with the cited studies. However, as with all literature reviews, the accuracy depends on correct interpretation of the cited work, which cannot be fully verified without examining each source.

results.result: Prior research and established neuroscience knowledge indicate that birth weight differences have been reported for neurodevelopmental disorders (ADHD, schizophrenia), that neurogenesis occurs almost exclusively during fetal development with severely restricted adult neurogenesis, that environmental adversity effects on epigenetic programming may be localized to the in utero period, and that various environmental factors (opioid exposure, air pollution) are associated with reduced birth weight.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 and C70-C78 cite relevant prior research to contextualize the findings. The neuroscience claims about neurogenesis (C71-C74) represent well-established knowledge supported by appropriate citations. The claims about environmental factors affecting birth weight (C76-C78) are supported by citations and provide public health context. These claims appropriately frame the discussion but are not directly tested in the current study.

results.result: Only persons with longitudinal MRI scans were included in the main analyses to limit the possibility that estimates of change were biased by immediate sample selection effects.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 describes an important methodological decision with clear rationale. This inclusion criterion is appropriate for longitudinal studies where attrition is non-random. However, this criterion itself introduces selection bias by excluding participants with only baseline data, who may differ systematically from those with follow-up. The authors acknowledge this trade-off, and the decision is reasonable for the study's focus on longitudinal change.

results.result: Birth weight shows remarkably stable and lifelong positive associations with cortical surface area and volume across all three cohorts (LCBC, ABCD, UKB), with widespread effects across most of the cortical mantle. The topography of these effects was highly consistent and replicable across datasets, with spatial correlations highest for volume (r=0.64-0.79) and high for area (r=0.51-0.71).
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. The editor states the study provides 'solid evidence that birth weight is associated with robust and persistent variations in cortical anatomy.' Reviewer 1 notes 'Prior studies have firmly established robust positive associations between BW and cortical SA, but this study adds evidence for the protracted lifespan persistence of these associations.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'BW is positively associated with cortical area (and, as a consequence, cortical volume) across most of the cortex' and praises the use of 'formal spatial analysis to quantify the reproducibility of effects across cohorts.'

results.result: Birth weight showed no consistent effect on cortical changes over time. Birth weight × time interactions were observed only in restricted, non-overlapping regions across samples, and spatial correlations of maps capturing birth weight-associated cortical change were either unrelated or showed negative associations between cohorts.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding as a key contribution. The editor notes 'less-substantial influences on cortical change over time.' Reviewer 1 states 'The results presented clearly establish that such BW-change associations are much more localized and less consistent across cohorts that BW-intercept associations' and emphasizes this as 'the primary way in which this work seeks to extend beyond established findings.' Reviewer 2 confirms the authors 'find that BW is positively associated with cortical area...with effect sizes greatest in frontal and temporal regions' but does not challenge the longitudinal findings.

results.result: Birth weight had lesser effects on cortical thickness compared to cortical area, with no significant effects on thickness observed in the UKB cohort. Spatial correlations for thickness effects were moderate (r=0.24-0.45) compared to area and volume.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without challenge. Reviewer 1 notes the study's strength in 'disambiguation of SA and CT findings,' implicitly accepting the differential effects. Reviewer 2 describes the study as examining 'area, volume and thickness of the cerebral cortex' without raising concerns about the thickness findings. The moderate spatial correlations for thickness are presented as part of the overall pattern of results that reviewers find convincing.

results.result: Analysis of monozygotic twin birth weight discordance indicated partly environmental effects on cortical characteristics. Heavier twins had greater cortical area in frontal, temporal, and occipitotemporal regions (right hemisphere effects surviving correction), while lighter twins showed greater thickness in restricted right frontotemporal regions. No effects were found on volume or longitudinal changes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the twin discordance findings. The editor's summary mentions the study uses 'multiple large neuroimaging datasets' with 'robust statistical methods,' which encompasses the twin analysis. Reviewer 1 notes the study's 'use of three large neuroimaging datasets' and 'multiple complementary approaches to verify the robustness of this inference,' which would include the twin analysis. No reviewer raises concerns about the environmental interpretation from twin data.

results.result: Sensitivity analyses showed that controlling for education level, gestational age, and restricting samples to birth weights between 2.5-5.0 kg had little effect on results. Significant positive effects of birth weight on cortical area remained when controlling for intracranial volume, particularly in lateral temporal and frontal areas.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise the sensitivity analyses. Reviewer 1 lists 'inclusion of sensible sensitivity analyses' as a study strength. Reviewer 2 notes 'These associations remain largely unchanged when accounting for age, sex, length of gestation and (in one cohort) ethnicity' and that 'Measures are taken to determine within sample replicability through split-half analyses.' The robustness checks are viewed as strengthening the main findings.

results.result: Effect size quantification showed that 1 SD lower birth weight (600-700g) was associated with 1.1-1.6% lesser cortical volume across cohorts (5980-8466 mm³), which could be quantitatively equal to 6-7.5 years of estimated age-related differences in cortical volume.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these quantitative estimates. Reviewer 2 notes 'effect sizes greatest in frontal and temporal regions,' acknowledging the quantification of effects. The editor describes the findings as providing 'solid evidence' with 'robust statistical methods,' which encompasses these effect size calculations. The comparison to age-related differences is presented as contextualizing the magnitude of birth weight effects.

results.result: The authors conclude that the influence of prenatal growth on cortical topography is stable and reliable through the lifespan, affecting the brain through brain reserve rather than brain maintenance mechanisms, with fetal influences appearing omnipresent in the spacetime of the human brain.
results.evaluation: Reviewers support these interpretive conclusions. The editor states the findings 'illustrate the long temporal reach of early developmental influences.' Reviewer 1 describes the work as providing 'a valuable new data point in our understanding of the profound and protracted influences that prenatal developmental features can have on postnatal outcomes.' Reviewer 2 concludes 'BW, as a marker of early development, is associated with brain characteristics throughout the lifespan,' directly affirming the persistence claim.

results.result: The study included 5718-5794 persons with 12,088 brain MRIs across three cohorts (LCBC: 635 participants, 1922 scans; ABCD: 3324 participants, 6648 scans; UKB: 1759 participants, 3518 scans), including 386 monozygotic twins, followed for up to 8.3 years, spanning ages 4-82 years.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise the sample characteristics. The editor describes it as using 'multiple large neuroimaging datasets acquired at different points through the lifespan.' Reviewer 1 lists 'use of three large neuroimaging datasets' as a key strength. Reviewer 2 states the study is 'supported by evidence from a large sample drawn from three geographically distinct cohorts' and notes the datasets 'together span childhood to late adulthood.' No concerns are raised about sample size or composition.

results.result: Cortical surfaces were reconstructed using FreeSurfer (v6.0 for LCBC/UKB, v7.1 for ABCD), with vertex-wise analyses using spatiotemporal linear mixed effects modeling, controlling for baseline age, sex, scanner site, time, and ethnicity (ABCD only).
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the methodological approach. The editor describes 'robust statistical methods.' Reviewer 1 praises the 'clearly motivation of this work' and notes the study's strengths without challenging the analytical methods. Reviewer 2 states the study has 'robust analytical and statistical methods' and notes 'Variations due to MRI scanner and site are accounted for statistically.' The methods are viewed as appropriate and rigorous.

results.result: The authors suggest that optimizing fetal growth may increase brain reserve for life, including in aging, and that programs and policies to limit environmental factors reducing fetal growth may enhance brain reserve and prevent functional decline in advanced age.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these implications without challenge. The editor states the findings 'carry relevance for how we conceptualize, study, and potentially modify such influences more generally,' directly supporting the policy implications. Reviewer 1 describes the work as having implications for 'how we conceptualize, study, and potentially modify' early developmental influences. No reviewer questions the translational or policy suggestions as overreaching.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on sample characteristics (C2-C5, C82-C92). Both evaluations affirm the large sample sizes, age ranges, and geographic diversity as study strengths. OpenEval emphasizes internal consistency of demographic data, while peer reviewers praise the use of multiple large datasets spanning childhood to late adulthood.

Strong agreement on baseline birth weight effects (C6, C29-C30, C33, C63-C64). Both evaluations support the robust associations between birth weight and cortical area/volume. OpenEval emphasizes high spatial correlations (r=0.51-0.79) and replicability across cohorts. Peer reviewers describe this as 'solid evidence' with 'protracted lifespan persistence.' OpenEval R2 also addresses spatial correlation claims (C41-C45) that overlap with peer R1.

Perfect agreement on lack of consistent longitudinal effects (C7, C38-C40, C46, C68). Both evaluations affirm this as a key finding. OpenEval highlights negative/near-zero spatial correlations (r=-0.35 to 0.04) for change effects. Peer reviewers emphasize this as 'the primary way in which this work seeks to extend beyond established findings' and note effects are 'much more localized and less consistent across cohorts.'

Agreement on differential thickness effects (C31-C32). Both evaluations support the finding of moderate correlations for thickness compared to area/volume. OpenEval notes absence of significant thickness effects in UKB. Peer reviewers accept these findings, with Reviewer 1 praising 'disambiguation of SA and CT findings.' Peer R3 also includes C45 (spatial correlation for thickness).

Perfect agreement on twin discordance analyses (C8, C47-C52). Both evaluations support the environmental interpretation from twin data. OpenEval notes the meta-analysis showed only suggestive (not statistically significant) spatial correspondence, adding appropriate caution. Peer reviewers accept the findings without challenge, viewing the twin analysis as part of 'multiple complementary approaches.'

Perfect agreement on sensitivity analyses (C34-C37). Both evaluations affirm these robustness checks strengthen the main findings. OpenEval details specific analyses (gestational age, sex interactions, outliers, ICV correction). Peer reviewers explicitly praise 'inclusion of sensible sensitivity analyses' and note measures remain 'largely unchanged' across sensitivity tests.

Agreement on spatial correlation analyses (C41-C45). Both evaluations support these methodological findings. OpenEval emphasizes the use of spin tests for appropriate statistical control. Peer reviewers praise the 'formal spatial analysis to quantify the reproducibility of effects across cohorts.' These claims overlap with peer R1's broader assessment of baseline effects.

Perfect agreement on effect size quantification (C53-C62). Both evaluations accept these calculations. OpenEval notes the comparison to age-related differences is illustrative and cautions against causal interpretation. Peer reviewers acknowledge 'effect sizes greatest in frontal and temporal regions' and view the quantification as part of 'robust statistical methods' without raising concerns.

Perfect agreement on interpretive conclusions about brain reserve (C9-C11, C69). Both evaluations support the distinction between baseline effects and lack of longitudinal change.
